why: This is a tree problem whose answer is monotone: if height h is reachable with k cuts, so is h+1. So binary search h, and check each h with a bottom-up tree pass that cuts a subtree only when keeping it would push something below depth h.
hints: If you can reach height h with at most max_operations moves, can you also reach h+1? That monotonicity suggests guessing h and checking it.

For a fixed h, process nodes from the deepest up. Track each node's subtree height. When a node v (whose parent is not the root) has subtree height h-1, keeping it would make some node deeper than h, so cut v and move it under the root, where it now fits exactly. Cutting as late (as high) as possible is the greedy choice.
Root the tree at 1 (edges are given unordered), get a BFS/DFS order, then binary search h in [1, n-1] with the O(n) greedy check. Total O(n log n).
pitfalls: The edge list is not oriented: tree_from[i] is not necessarily the parent. Build an undirected adjacency list and root it at 1.
Children of the root never need cutting; moving them changes nothing.
Use an iterative traversal; a path-shaped tree overflows Python's recursion limit.
Height is counted in edges, so a single node has height 0.
constraints:
• 2 ≤ tree_nodes ≤ 10^5 (not stated in the source; typical for this OA)
  • 0 ≤ max_operations ≤ tree_nodes - 1
  • The edges form a tree on tables 1..tree_nodes; edge direction is not guaranteed to be parent to child.
